title: NFL’s underrated, overrated teams: NFL South could rise; Bears, Bills, Patriots tumble The Falcons, Panthers and Saints could be better than expected, while regression is logical for two of 2025's biggest surprise teams. Mike Jones
summary:

It’s one of the best times of year according to the NFL calendar. In a matter of days, training camp will have opened across the league, and all 32 teams — brimming with lofty expectations — will hit the fields to lay the foundation for their upcoming campaigns.
Ten teams have new head coaches, more than half the league features new offens
full_text:
Bijan Robinson's Falcons could be a surprise contender, while Christian Benford's Bills might regress with a new coach in charge. Todd Kirkland / Getty Images
It’s one of the best times of year according to the NFL calendar. In a matter of days, training camp will have opened across the league, and all 32 teams — brimming with lofty expectations — will hit the fields to lay the foundation for their upcoming campaigns.
Ten teams have new head coaches, more than half the league features new offensive coordinators and just less than half welcome defensive coordinators this offseason.
The free-agent acquisitions and draft selections have begun to settle into their new surroundings, and now they get to work.
While every player and coach aspires to contend for the Super Bowl, expectations differ depending on the team. Some highly-touted squads will live up to their potential while others will fall short. Others will exceed expectations and make life difficult for opponents.
We’re taking a look at some of the most underrated and overrated teams entering the 2026 season and how things could shake out for them.
The Falcons are among the 10 teams that hired new head coaches this offseason, but the cupboard is far from bare. Raheem Morris led the Falcons on a four-game winning streak that helped them finish 8-9 and tie with the Carolina Panthers and Tampa Bay Buccaneers atop the NFC South, but it came after they had already been eliminated from playoff contention based on potential tiebreakers.
Arthur Blank opted for change, and Kevin Stefanski inherits a team that features plenty of talent, with Bijan Robinson, Kyle Pitts, Drake London, A.J. Terrell, Jessie Bates III, James Pearce and Xavier Watts leading the way. If he can figure out the quarterback situation (Michael Penix Jr. versus Tua Tagovailoa) and keep one of those two on the field, Atlanta could challenge for the division.
Had Daniel Jones not ruptured his Achilles tendon in Week 14, Shane Steichen’s squad very well may have contended for the top seed in the AFC. The Colts expect Jones to open the season, and they hope he can pick up where he left off and help direct a top-10 offense that still boasts a strong line and running back Jonathan Taylor. The Colts have a tough opening schedule , but could certainly contend in the AFC South.
A 31st-ranked defense that surrendered at least 30 points in seven contests and more than 45 points twice offered next to no support for an offense that endured a nine-game stretch without a healthy Joe Burrow. Now the franchise quarterback returns, and the additions of defensive tackles Dexter Lawrence and Jonathan Allen and pass rusher Boye Mafe should help bolster Cincinnati’s defensive front.
Thanks to those moves, plus others along the defense, the Bengals just might have better depth than they did when they reached the Super Bowl during the 2021 season. The Baltimore Ravens draw much attention in the AFC North, and rightfully so, and Mike McCarthy’s reunion with Aaron Rodgers in Pittsburgh has the Steelers in the spotlight, but the Bengals seem primed for a bounce-back season and could cause trouble for divisional foes.
A tiebreaker over the Buccaneers and Falcons paved the way for the Panthers’ first playoff appearance in eight years. Bryce Young’s third season saw him put up career numbers in passing yards (3,011) and touchdowns (23). The defense went from dead last to middle of the pack. Despite pushing the Los Angeles Rams in a 34-31 wild-card loss, the Panthers continue to fly under the radar.
General manager Dan Morgan was busy, making moves to upgrade both the offensive and defensive fronts, adding veteran guards in Robert Hunt and Damien Lewis, and pass rusher Jaelan Phillips and linebacker Devin Lloyd. Carolina coach Dave Canales and his group just might make some more strides in his third season.
There’s not a lot of sizzle about the Saints, but rookie head coach Kellen Moore did help guide his squad forward last season, especially during a 4-0 December. They will need some players to grow into roles on defense, but on offense, if second-year quarterback Tyler Shough can build on his late-season progress and capitalize on the additions of rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson and running back Travis Etienne to a unit that already includes Chris Olave and Alvin Kamara, the Saints, who split with the Bucs and swept the Panthers last season, could make some noise in the division.
Jerry Jones will tell you the Cowboys always have a shot at contention, and his team does generate plenty of buzz. But the Cowboys will have to jell in a hurry on defense, where new defensive coordinator Christian Parker inherits a unit that struggled mightily last season but added plenty of new faces, including veterans like pass rusher Rashan Gary, cornerback Cobie Durant, linebacker Dee Winters and rookie linebackers Malachi Lawrence and Jaishawn Barham. The offense, led by Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, should again put up points, but the much-needed defensive backing could take some time.
The Bills came up painfully short in their quest for a Super Bowl, and coach Sean McDermott got fired. They’re regarded as contenders largely because Josh Allen is always darting in and out of phone booths. But it’s well documented that he can’t do it alone. The Bills could experience some growing pains as Joe Brady attempts to make the big jump from offensive coordinator to head coach, and new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard tries to install a brand-new defense.
Ben Johnson ignited the Bears in his first season at the helm, and he helped Caleb Williams tap into some of the potential the franchise saw in the quarterback when selecting him No. 1 in 2024. Chicago’s defense led the NFL with 33 takeaways, and the Bears leapfrogged the Minnesota Vikings, Green Bay Packers and Detroit Lions in the division and reached the divisional round of the playoffs.
Expectations have skyrocketed, but taking that next step represents a great challenge. Williams delivered late-game heroics, but he and his team can’t count on a repeat of that trend. He’ll have to improve his consistency by a significant margin, and Chicago’s defense can’t get away with such a low pressure rate and such struggles against the run. The Bears feel primed for a step backward rather than forward.
The Eagles have ranked among the elite teams of the NFC for the last 10 years, making the playoffs nine times and winning the Super Bowl twice. Even with last season’s regression, they won the NFC East for the third time in four seasons.
But now they’re trying to re-tool on the fly, subtracting the disgruntled A.J. Brown and drafting Makai Lemon, rolling with their fourth offensive coordinator in as many years (rookie play caller Sean Mannion), and adding veterans Jonathan Greenard and Riq Woolen on defense while losing standouts Nakobe Dean and Reed Blankenship. The health of the offensive line is a concern, as is a tough late-season stretch . Although viewed as a bar-setter, the Eagles could hit a few snags this season.
The Patriots certainly exceeded expectations in 2025, overtaking Buffalo for the division and reaching the Super Bowl, where they lost to the Seattle Seahawks. Mike Vrabel and his players badly want to resolve unfinished business in 2026, but doing so could prove challenging.
New England will not have the luxury of sneaking up on teams this season. The Patriots also have a grueling start , with three road games in their first four weeks and two back-to-back road trips in their first 10 weeks. The Patriots landed A.J. Brown in hopes that he can help elevate Drake Maye, but chemistry could take some time. New England also still seems to lack a game-changing pass rush, which needs to change for their defense to take another step forward.

title: Ranking Ravens' top training camp storylines: Will Nnamdi Madubuike make a return? Plus, will Baltimore's defense get its swagger back under Jesse Minter? And how will Lamar Jackson's partnership with OC Declan Doyle evolve? Jeff Zrebiec

full_text:
Ravens two-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike played in just two games last season due to a neck injury. Katie Stratman / Imagn Images
Jesse Minter’s inaugural training camp as an NFL head coach officially begins with the Baltimore Ravens’ first full-squad practice on July 29. After 18 John Harbaugh-led training camps, this is being appropriately billed as a new era of Ravens football.
While the influence of Minter and a mostly new coaching staff will be highly scrutinized throughout the summer, there are plenty of other storylines as Baltimore looks to move further beyond last year’s disappointing season and get back into the AFC playoff mix.
There’s a star quarterback again facing contract questions, a rebuilt offensive line, a key defensive player with a still-uncertain future, a new star edge rusher and a host of young players trying to establish themselves as Ravens mainstays.
Let’s rank the 10 biggest storylines of the summer as the Ravens prepare to get back to work.
The addition of edge rusher Trey Hendrickson should pay immediate dividends. Veteran safety Jaylinn Hawkins looks like a perfect complement to Kyle Hamilton and Malaki Starks. First-round guard Vega Ioane was drafted to be an impact starter from the jump. However, a case could be made that the biggest addition the Ravens could have is a healthy Madubuike.
The two-time Pro Bowler missed all but two games last season because of a significant neck injury. The Ravens have been mostly mum about his status, but general manager Eric DeCosta said last week in an interview with 105.7 The Fan that things are “pointed in the right direction.” That’s the most optimistic comment a team official has given publicly on Madubuike’s status since the injury.
Madubuike had neck surgery in April and hasn’t been cleared medically by team doctors to return to the field. That would be the first step in what’s been a challenging road back for the 28-year-old. If Madubuike gets the green light, the Ravens will then evaluate how much time he needs before he’s on the same schedule as his teammates.
It will take months, if not years, to fairly judge the Ravens’ decision to move on from Harbaugh and replace him with one of his former assistants. Yet, Minter’s immediate impact will surely be documented over the next two months, as will the changes he makes in the way the Ravens practice and prepare, and in how he leads the team and handles head-coaching duties.
Some of Minter’s changes were instituted in the offseason workouts. Warmups were different. A “be at your best when your best is required” phase was added at the end of practices. Minter made a change in moving the start of training camp practices to the morning, when they were almost exclusively in the afternoon in recent years.
What remains to be seen is whether camp practices are structured differently, how Minter handles the summer workload for veterans, how much, if any, starters play in the preseason and, generally, how a team loaded with accomplished veterans responds to Minter during the summer grind. Players have been effusive about Minter and the new coaching so far, but training camp brings a different set of circumstances.
There is understandable curiosity in how the Ravens’ new offense — and defense, for that matter — will take shape. Training camp, however, probably won’t yield a ton of answers. Minter and Doyle, Baltimore’s first-year play caller, presumably won’t show a lot in open practices and games. They’ll want to keep their regular-season opponents in suspense.
What will be on full display daily is how Jackson and Doyle interact, how Doyle goes about getting his offense ready for the season and how sharp the offense is throughout the summer. Per the team’s media policy, reporters aren’t allowed to say or write tactical info, such as formations and which players are taking reps with which units, but training camp should at least give some clues to how things will look come Sept. 13 when the Ravens open against the Indianapolis Colts.
All indications are that Jackson and the new coaching staff have hit it off and he’s excited about the future of the offense. However, given last year’s tumult, the dynamic between Jackson and Doyle and Minter will be particularly interesting to watch.
Owner Steve Bisciotti was open earlier this offseason about wanting to extend Jackson as soon as possible. More than six months later, there is still no deal and no indication that one is close, although the Ravens and Jackson have succeeded in keeping any news about the negotiations — or lack thereof — out of the media. Thus, little is known about whether DeCosta and Jackson are negotiating or have any plans to address his contract before the season.
Jackson, whose contract was restructured in March, is signed through 2027. His cap hit next year is a whopping $84.3 million. Each passing month without a new deal will only increase the speculation about Jackson’s future in Baltimore, so a preseason extension would lift a lot of angst for the organization.
As for Flowers, he’s also signed through 2027. He’s said he wants to sign an extension to remain in Baltimore, and the Ravens want that, too. Now, they have to get it done at a time when wide receiver salaries are skyrocketing.
Free-agent signing John Simpson will be the new starter at left guard. Ioane will take over for Daniel Faalele at right guard. Tyler Linderbaum’s replacement at center will likely be free-agent signing Ethan Pocic . If he’s not ready to return from an Achilles injury, another free-agent addition, Danny Pinter, would probably get the nod. Dwayne Ledford, highly thought of around the league and an assistant DeCosta and Minter coveted during the hiring process, is the new offensive line coach.
All told, the Ravens signed four free-agent offensive linemen, drafted two and then added two more as undrafted free agents. That’s a lot of change, but it also wasn’t surprising. Fixing an offensive line that struggled for much of last year was one of DeCosta’s biggest offseason priorities. Now, it’s up to Ledford to develop the young linemen and get the group to play to its potential.
If Jackson stays healthy and the offensive line is much improved, the Ravens will again have one of the league’s top offenses.
The Ravens believe he has, and if they didn’t, they presumably would have signed another kicker to at least serve as competition for Loop in camp. Loop, whose 44-yard miss in Week 18 kept Baltimore out of the playoffs and ended an uneven rookie season, insists his confidence is in a good place and he kicked well in offseason practices.
Still, Loop is a few bad practices or a few preseason misses away from the questions about how the Ravens can rely on him getting even louder. There is probably no Raven, except Jackson, who will be scrutinized more this summer than Loop. It’s an unenviable position to be in, but Loop needs to deliver.
Baltimore’s decision-makers insist they had no preference between an offensive, defensive or special teams-minded head coach. They wanted the best candidate and the best fit. Hiring a coach who could fix the defense, though, made a great deal of sense, particularly because you already know that if Jackson is healthy, the offense is going to be good.
Minter and defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver have a lot to work with. They also have a lot to fix from last year, when the Ravens defense couldn’t consistently mount a pass rush, had too many breakdowns on the back end and struggled to close games. It was a huge letdown for an organization that was built around a suffocating defense.
Minter’s defensive system has been highly successful wherever he’s been. A defensive resurgence, however, will start with getting middle linebacker Roquan Smith, cornerback Marlon Humphrey and Madubuike (assuming he returns) back to their Pro Bowl form. The free-agent acquisitions and draft selections have begun to settle into their new surroundings, and now they get to work.
While every player and coach aspires to contend for the Super Bowl, expectations differ depending on the team. Some highly-touted squads will live up to their potential while others will fall short. Others will exceed expectations and make life difficult for opponents.
We’re taking a look at some of the most underrated and overrated teams entering the 2026 season and how things could shake out for them.
The Falcons are among the 10 teams that hired new head coaches this offseason, but the cupboard is far from bare. Raheem Morris led the Falcons on a four-game winning streak that helped them finish 8-9 and tie with the Carolina Panthers and Tampa Bay Buccaneers atop the NFC South, but it came after they had already been eliminated from playoff contention based on potential tiebreakers.
Arthur Blank opted for change, and Kevin Stefanski inherits a team that features plenty of talent, with Bijan Robinson, Kyle Pitts, Drake London, A.J. Terrell, Jessie Bates III, James Pearce and Xavier Watts leading the way. If he can figure out the quarterback situation (Michael Penix Jr. versus Tua Tagovailoa) and keep one of those two on the field, Atlanta could challenge for the division.
Had Daniel Jones not ruptured his Achilles tendon in Week 14, Shane Steichen’s squad very well may have contended for the top seed in the AFC. The Colts expect Jones to open the season, and they hope he can pick up where he left off and help direct a top-10 offense that still boasts a strong line and running back Jonathan Taylor. The Colts have a tough opening schedule , but could certainly contend in the AFC South.
A 31st-ranked defense that surrendered at least 30 points in seven contests and more than 45 points twice offered next to no support for an offense that endured a nine-game stretch without a healthy Joe Burrow. Now the franchise quarterback returns, and the additions of defensive tackles Dexter Lawrence and Jonathan Allen and pass rusher Boye Mafe should help bolster Cincinnati’s defensive front.
Thanks to those moves, plus others along the defense, the Bengals just might have better depth than they did when they reached the Super Bowl during the 2021 season. The Baltimore Ravens draw much attention in the AFC North, and rightfully so, and Mike McCarthy’s reunion with Aaron Rodgers in Pittsburgh has the Steelers in the spotlight, but the Bengals seem primed for a bounce-back season and could cause trouble for divisional foes.
A tiebreaker over the Buccaneers and Falcons paved the way for the Panthers’ first playoff appearance in eight years. Bryce Young’s third season saw him put up career numbers in passing yards (3,011) and touchdowns (23). The defense went from dead last to middle of the pack. Despite pushing the Los Angeles Rams in a 34-31 wild-card loss, the Panthers continue to fly under the radar.
General manager Dan Morgan was busy, making moves to upgrade both the offensive and defensive fronts, adding veteran guards in Robert Hunt and Damien Lewis, and pass rusher Jaelan Phillips and linebacker Devin Lloyd. Carolina coach Dave Canales and his group just might make some more strides in his third season.
There’s not a lot of sizzle about the Saints, but rookie head coach Kellen Moore did help guide his squad forward last season, especially during a 4-0 December. They will need some players to grow into roles on defense, but on offense, if second-year quarterback Tyler Shough can build on his late-season progress and capitalize on the additions of rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson and running back Travis Etienne to a unit that already includes Chris Olave and Alvin Kamara, the Saints, who split with the Bucs and swept the Panthers last season, could make some noise in the division.
Jerry Jones will tell you the Cowboys always have a shot at contention, and his team does generate plenty of buzz. But the Cowboys will have to jell in a hurry on defense, where new defensive coordinator Christian Parker inherits a unit that struggled mightily last season but added plenty of new faces, including veterans like pass rusher Rashan Gary, cornerback Cobie Durant, linebacker Dee Winters and rookie linebackers Malachi Lawrence and Jaishawn Barham. The offense, led by Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, should again put up points, but the much-needed defensive backing could take some time.
The Bills came up painfully short in their quest for a Super Bowl, and coach Sean McDermott got fired. They’re regarded as contenders largely because Josh Allen is always darting in and out of phone booths. But it’s well documented that he can’t do it alone. The Bills could experience some growing pains as Joe Brady attempts to make the big jump from offensive coordinator to head coach, and new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard tries to install a brand-new defense.
Ben Johnson ignited the Bears in his first season at the helm, and he helped Caleb Williams tap into some of the potential the franchise saw in the quarterback when selecting him No. 1 in 2024. Chicago’s defense led the NFL with 33 takeaways, and the Bears leapfrogged the Minnesota Vikings, Green Bay Packers and Detroit Lions in the division and reached the divisional round of the playoffs.
Expectations have skyrocketed, but taking that next step represents a great challenge. Williams delivered late-game heroics, but he and his team can’t count on a repeat of that trend. He’ll have to improve his consistency by a significant margin, and Chicago’s defense can’t get away with such a low pressure rate and such struggles against the run. The Bears feel primed for a step backward rather than forward.
The Eagles have ranked among the elite teams of the NFC for the last 10 years, making the playoffs nine times and winning the Super Bowl twice. Even with last season’s regression, they won the NFC East for the third time in four seasons.

Brown and drafting Makai Lemon, rolling with their fourth offensive coordinator in as many years (rookie play caller Sean Mannion), and adding veterans Jonathan Greenard and Riq Woolen on defense while losing standouts Nakobe Dean and Reed Blankenship. The health of the offensive line is a concern, as is a tough late-season stretch . Although viewed as a bar-setter, the Eagles could hit a few snags this season.
The Patriots certainly exceeded expectations in 2025, overtaking Buffalo for the division and reaching the Super Bowl, where they lost to the Seattle Seahawks. Mike Vrabel and his players badly want to resolve unfinished business in 2026, but doing so could prove challenging.
New England will not have the luxury of sneaking up on teams this season. The Patriots also have a grueling start , with three road games in their first four weeks and two back-to-back road trips in their first 10 weeks. The Patriots landed A.J. Brown in hopes that he can help elevate Drake Maye, but chemistry could take some time. New England also still seems to lack a game-changing pass rush, which needs to change for their defense to take another step forward.

title: Bengals roster assessment: Which 8 players can Cincinnati least afford to lose? We're not ranking the Bengals' best players. We're calculating their importance based on the depth chart, impact on scheme and much more. Paul Dehner Jr.
summary:
Three of the Bengals' most important players: wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase, quarterback Joe Burrow and wide receiver Tee Higgins. Sam Greene / Imagn Images
One question lingers throughout the haze of every NFL August: Did anyone get hurt?
Every team simply wants to make it through training camp and preseason healthy. Yet, every year, dozens of players around the league suffer injuries that send the season off the tracks before it even begins. Some losses, of course, are more critical than others.
full_text:
Three of the Bengals' most important players: wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase, quarterback Joe Burrow and wide receiver Tee Higgins. Sam Greene / Imagn Images
One question lingers throughout the haze of every NFL August: Did anyone get hurt?
Every team simply wants to make it through training camp and preseason healthy. Yet, every year, dozens of players around the league suffer injuries that send the season off the tracks before it even begins. Some losses, of course, are more critical than others.
A preseason exercise I’ve enjoyed doing over the years involves assigning a value to Cincinnati Bengals players by using my own Wins Above Replacement (WAR) figure, a stat typically associated with baseball.
The WAR ranking of a player filters down to how many more games the team would lose without them in the regular season.
That’s not as simple as ranking the best players — not by a long shot. That formula is calculated by the quality of their backup, impact on the scheme, leadership fallout, roster construction, positional importance and, yes, talent level.
I’ve ranked them one through eight, as well as by tiers, to categorize the impact of a potential injury. The WAR number is games lost if the player missed all 17 regular-season games.
So, who can the Bengals least afford to lose?
WAR: 4.0 Games played past three years: 35 of 51
Background: Say hello to Joe Flacco: a walking, talking $6 million insurance policy. That’s why he’s here. All the injury history with Burrow and investment in the passing game pushed the Bengals to be hyper-aggressive in landing a quality backup . Flacco played well last year in Cincinnati despite learning on the fly midseason following the trade from Cleveland.
Stat: Over the past three years, the Bengals are 19-16 in games Burrow starts and 5-11 in games he doesn’t, including a 1-8 mark in 2025.
Bottom line: No secrets here. If you could tell the Bengals this season would be one of the more injury-marred campaigns in recent years, but Burrow would play every snap, they’d likely sign on for that. But if you knew you’d only lose Burrow for a month, the club feels confident Flacco could keep things afloat. But his presence doesn’t change the reality that Burrow must stay healthy for the Bengals to meet expectations.
Flacco's 'Unc Bowl' performance is even crazier when you know the full context 🤯
Formation and headset issues didn't stop Joe from dropping 350 yard and 3 TDs pic.twitter.com/8CfA8jc6cd
— NFL Films (@NFLFilms) July 16, 2026
WAR: 3.0 Games played past three years: 48 of 51
Background: Employing both Chase and Tee Higgins makes the Bengals’ passing game nearly unstoppable when they are both on the field. It also makes life easier if one sustains a ding during the year. Higgins has dealt with more injuries than Chase in recent seasons, but the offense can still sing with Burrow and one of the team’s two great receivers.
The concern with losing Chase is how much the offense revolves around his gravity. Cincinnati started moving Chase around the formation as much as any player in football in 2024 and hasn’t stopped. So much of what the Bengals do revolves around the attention teams pay to him and how they deal with his movement before the snap. That, coupled with his immense talent and chemistry with Burrow, puts him in Tier 1.
Stat: Chase has played the third-most snaps in the NFL over the past three years, and outside of a hip injury that kept him out a month in 2022, he has never missed extended time.
Bottom line: Anything can happen in football, of course, but Chase is a near-indestructible robot built in an elite receiver lab. The Bengals need that to continue.
WAR: 2.5 Games played past three years: 45 of 51
Background: Turner broke out in 2025, establishing himself as one of the game’s premier cover corners. He followed the opposing team’s best receivers around the field the majority of the season to resounding levels of success. A lucrative contract could be coming his way because of it.
His lofty spot in these rankings is as much about his performance as the cliff behind him. On the depth chart beyond Turner, there are a collection of rookies, journeymen and unprovens. Any one of them, if forced to start, would be the focus of the opposing offensive coordinator’s game plan. The depth behind Turner (and Dax Hill) is a glaring issue and a critical concern during camp.
Stat: Turner has never started an opener for the Bengals, even though he was healthy each of his past three seasons.
Bottom line: Turner broke his collarbone and missed the final six games of the 2024 season, but other than that has shown durability despite being a smaller player (5-foot-11, 185 pounds). The Bengals need his health more than ever this year (or third-round pick Tacario Davis will have to figure things out in a hurry).
WAR: 2.0 Game played past two years: 32 of 34
Background: Mims looks like the next great player on this Bengals’ offense. He’s grown into his body, dominated the second half of last season and possesses All-Pro potential. An offensive line that’s been without a true star since Andrew Whitworth departed might finally have one.
Also, the backup situation is shaky. The Bengals hope Cody Ford can regain the confidence they had in him when he played well in the stretch run of 2024, but he fell out of favor (and shape) last season. We’ll find out if he’s in a better place this year, as he focuses on trying to win Cincinnati’s swing tackle job.
If that goes well, Mims drops down a tier in these rankings. For now, he’s essential to keeping the offense running.
Stat: Mims did not allow a sack or QB hit once Burrow returned for the final six games of last season.
Bottom line: The Bengals are working on unlocking him as a weapon beyond just dominant pass protection, and that makes him key for a scheme that puts more pressure on its tackles to protect in true pass sets.
WAR: 1.5 Games played past three years: 45 of 51
Background: Lawrence might be the hardest to judge without seeing how all the new defensive pieces fit together in practice. In theory, Lawrence looks to be the central piece around which all others move. The pass rush will revolve around his ability to draw double teams. Along the defensive line, his presence will be counted on to augment the production of the Jonathan Allen-BJ Hill combination, each of whom is playing in their age 31 seasons. Lawrence will also be critical to the second-year jumps for linebackers Barrett Carter and Demetrius Knight Jr.
T.J. Slaton was last year’s starter and the current backup. He was solid, specifically against the run, but he won’t offer much juice as a pass rusher. He’s a more than adequate replacement, but Lawrence is being counted on to be a star.
Stat: Lawrence ranked fourth in pass-rush win percentage among interior defenders last season despite also ranking fifth in double-team percentage.
Bottom line: The combination of Lawrence and Slaton is, arguably, the best nose tackle lineup in the NFL. There’s a reason defensive coordinator Al Golden would build around it.
WAR: 1.5 Games played the past three years: 39 of 51
Background: Can you build a scary offense in the NFL around two players with valid availability concerns? The Bengals have done just that with Higgins catching passes from Burrow. There is zero questioning Higgins’ will or competitive fire. He’s played through injuries in huge moments over the years. Higgins’ issues have revolved around soft tissue ailments in his legs that creep up nearly every season. He’s sought advice, altered workout routines and consulted doctors to address the concerns, yet they have persisted. He also dealt with repeated concussions last year.
Over the past three years, Andrei Iosivas actually has played more snaps (1,913) than Higgins (1,880)
When he’s on the field, however, Higgins completely changes the dynamic of the Bengals’ offense. Teams just can’t compete with Chase and Higgins.

full_text:
Kerby Joseph's status entering training camp next week is unknown as the Lions' safety continues his recovery from a knee injury. Junfu Han / Imagn Images
It’s been a long offseason — longer than usual for the Detroit Lions after watching the playoffs from home — but training camp is just one week away.
Soon, rookies will report, veterans will return and we’ll get an early look at what Dan Campbell’s Lions have cooking for the 2026 season. Jobs will be won and lost over the next six weeks, as the Lions attempt to right the wrongs that led to a NFC North fourth-place finish in 2025. Campbell expects this to be the most competitive training camp the Lions have had in his six years as head coach. He thinks it’s necessary to get this team where it needs to be.
So then, which players have the most to lose and gain as the Lions re-emphasize competition?
Admittedly, this one is less about competition and more about availability. The 2025 season was a devastating one for Joseph. He missed extended time in training camp with a knee injury, left several games early in the season, was rested for weeks and suffered several setbacks when attempting to return to action. In total, Joseph missed 11 games last year, and we still don’t have a firm answer on the status of his knee injury.
“I honestly do not know,” Campbell said. “I know this, we’ve done everything we can do and he’s done everything he can do to this point. And we are trying to be as smart as we can and not push this until we absolutely have to because once we’ve done that, then we’ll know one way or another and it’s not worth it right now. We’re just slowly building, continuing the strength in there. He’s getting treatment. He’s done some of these different things at different places to try to help. So, I feel good about that. I feel good about that we’ve done everything we can. … I mean honestly, we probably won’t know until we get into the thick of training camp.”
Training camp is almost here, and it’s obvious that Joseph is the No. 1 player to watch when things kick off next week. What will his workload look like? Will he be limited? Will he be full-go or will the Lions ease him into things? Will they change their minds and delay his return until closer to the season? How will he look running and cutting? If Joseph looks like himself, the Lions will be getting back a difference-maker, which should alleviate some concerns about the secondary. He’s an All-Pro talent at his best, after all. But if the setbacks persist, it could create an uncomfortable conversation about his future in Detroit.
When the Lions released Terrion Arnold , Rakestraw immediately moved up the depth chart and finds himself with a real shot at playing time, in ways he didn’t previously. Rakestraw is just two years removed from a stellar training camp as a rookie playing nickel. He was sticky in coverage, made plays on the ball and his physicality was on full display. Those were the traits that made him a second-round pick in 2024, one round after Arnold was selected. Rakestraw told reporters at the end of the season that the coaching staff was ready to start him in Week 2 vs. the Bucs, but he suffered an injury in pregame warm-ups. It’s been the story of his career since.
Rakestraw missed the entire 2025 season after he underwent shoulder surgery. He’s back in action now, a bit bulkier than we last saw him, and earned some reps with the first-team defense during minicamp. Right now, Rock Ya-Sin feels like the next man up to replace Arnold, but Rakestraw will have every opportunity to earn the trust of the staff if he can manage to stay healthy. Emphasis on “if.”
There was plenty of optimism about Mahogany entering the starting lineup around this time last year. He filled in admirably in a couple spot-starts as a rookie, while missing his first NFL training camp with mononucleosis. The Lions needed to save money, and having a sixth-round guard with upside on a rookie contract made all the sense in the world. But last year, Mahogany looked like just that — a sixth-round guard with upside. He struggled in pass protection, spent time on injured reserve and probably wants nothing more than to put last season behind. However, unlike last season, the Lions now have competition at the position. The Lions signed veteran Ben Bartch, a player with 24 career starts. They have 2025 fifth-round pick Miles Frazier entering his second season. And while Juice Scruggs is better at center, he has guard experience. Given how much Campbell has preached competition, you have to think Mahogany won’t be handed the job.
That said, Mahogany should benefit from Drew Petzing’s system and playing next to players like Cade Mays and Penei Sewell this year vs. Graham Glasgow and an injured Taylor Decker last year. This is his job to lose.
We’ll group the Michigan rookies together for this one. Neither had to travel far to get to Detroit, and they might not have to wait long to see the field, either.
Let’s start with Moore. The Lions surprised some folks around the league when they selected Moore over players like Zion Young, Gabe Jacas and other edge rushers after trading up in the second round, but those who know this organization saw the fit. Moore was a captain at Michigan, won a national title, recorded 10 sacks and a pass-rush win rate of 20.5 percent — top 10 in the country — and can set an edge in the run game. The Lions signed D.J. Wonnum and believe he can benefit from playing opposite of an edge like Aidan Hutchinson, but Moore is the long-term play. When the pads go on, we’ll see how ready he is for the league.
Then there’s Rolder. The Lions let Alex Anzalone walk in free agency and re-signed Malcolm Rodriguez, who has the inside track at the position right now. But defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard and LBs coach Shaun Dion Hamilton aren’t afraid to play rookies. Rolder only has 11 career starts under his belt and he’s a bit slow to process in coverage, which might impact his playing time early. That said, Rolder displayed natural instincts and is a good athlete for his size. He impressed in OTAs and minicamp and seems to be a quick study. If he can pick up where he left off, he could make this a battle to watch.
When the Lions traded David Montgomery and signed Pacheco, most assumed the Lions had their 1-2 punch. Pacheco, when healthy, can do much of the dirty work for this offense as a physical runner and short-yardage option who can be a plus in pass pro. That said, he’ll need to prove his best days aren’t already behind him.
Per Warren Sharp, among RBs with at least 100 rush attempts last season, Pacheco ranked 46th in explosive run rate (3.4 percent), 47th in longest rush (16 yds on 118 attempts), 47th in success rate (29.7 percent) and 38th in YPC (3.9) despite facing the NFL’s highest rate of light boxes and lowest rate of seven- and eight-plus box defenders. It’s fair to wonder if Pacheco is still the same player he once was — even if the Lions don’t necessarily need him to be.
Now, Pacheco likely won’t have to lose sleep in training camp. There’s a role for him in this offense. But Sione Vaki was quietly putting together an excellent training camp last year when healthy. By all accounts, the hamstring isn’t an issue. He was available for OTAs and minicamp and should be next week as well. He’s a natural pass catcher, but if Vaki continues to develop, the opportunity is there for him to cut into Pacheco’s touches.

It’s one of the best times of year according to the NFL calendar. In a matter of days, training camp will have opened across the league, and all 32 teams — brimming with lofty expectations — will hit the fields to lay the foundation for their upcoming campaigns.
Ten teams have new head coaches, more than half the league features new offensive coordinators and just less than half welcome defensive coordinators this offseason.
The free-agent acquisitions and draft selections have begun to settle into their new surroundings, and now they get to work.
While every player and coach aspires to contend for the Super Bowl, expectations differ depending on the team. Some highly-touted squads will live up to their potential while others will fall short. Others will exceed expectations and make life difficult for opponents.
We’re taking a look at some of the most underrated and overrated teams entering the 2026 season and how things could shake out for them.
The Falcons are among the 10 teams that hired new head coaches this offseason, but the cupboard is far from bare. Raheem Morris led the Falcons on a four-game winning streak that helped them finish 8-9 and tie with the Carolina Panthers and Tampa Bay Buccaneers atop the NFC South, but it came after they had already been eliminated from playoff contention based on potential tiebreakers.
Arthur Blank opted for change, and Kevin Stefanski inherits a team that features plenty of talent, with Bijan Robinson, Kyle Pitts, Drake London, A.J. Terrell, Jessie Bates III, James Pearce and Xavier Watts leading the way. If he can figure out the quarterback situation (Michael Penix Jr. versus Tua Tagovailoa) and keep one of those two on the field, Atlanta could challenge for the division.
Had Daniel Jones not ruptured his Achilles tendon in Week 14, Shane Steichen’s squad very well may have contended for the top seed in the AFC. The Colts expect Jones to open the season, and they hope he can pick up where he left off and help direct a top-10 offense that still boasts a strong line and running back Jonathan Taylor. The Colts have a tough opening schedule , but could certainly contend in the AFC South.
A 31st-ranked defense that surrendered at least 30 points in seven contests and more than 45 points twice offered next to no support for an offense that endured a nine-game stretch without a healthy Joe Burrow. Now the franchise quarterback returns, and the additions of defensive tackles Dexter Lawrence and Jonathan Allen and pass rusher Boye Mafe should help bolster Cincinnati’s defensive front.
Thanks to those moves, plus others along the defense, the Bengals just might have better depth than they did when they reached the Super Bowl during the 2021 season. The Baltimore Ravens draw much attention in the AFC North, and rightfully so, and Mike McCarthy’s reunion with Aaron Rodgers in Pittsburgh has the Steelers in the spotlight, but the Bengals seem primed for a bounce-back season and could cause trouble for divisional foes.
A tiebreaker over the Buccaneers and Falcons paved the way for the Panthers’ first playoff appearance in eight years. Bryce Young’s third season saw him put up career numbers in passing yards (3,011) and touchdowns (23). The defense went from dead last to middle of the pack. Despite pushing the Los Angeles Rams in a 34-31 wild-card loss, the Panthers continue to fly under the radar.
General manager Dan Morgan was busy, making moves to upgrade both the offensive and defensive fronts, adding veteran guards in Robert Hunt and Damien Lewis, and pass rusher Jaelan Phillips and linebacker Devin Lloyd. Carolina coach Dave Canales and his group just might make some more strides in his third season.
There’s not a lot of sizzle about the Saints, but rookie head coach Kellen Moore did help guide his squad forward last season, especially during a 4-0 December. They will need some players to grow into roles on defense, but on offense, if second-year quarterback Tyler Shough can build on his late-season progress and capitalize on the additions of rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson and running back Travis Etienne to a unit that already includes Chris Olave and Alvin Kamara, the Saints, who split with the Bucs and swept the Panthers last season, could make some noise in the division.
Jerry Jones will tell you the Cowboys always have a shot at contention, and his team does generate plenty of buzz. But the Cowboys will have to jell in a hurry on defense, where new defensive coordinator Christian Parker inherits a unit that struggled mightily last season but added plenty of new faces, including veterans like pass rusher Rashan Gary, cornerback Cobie Durant, linebacker Dee Winters and rookie linebackers Malachi Lawrence and Jaishawn Barham. The offense, led by Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, should again put up points, but the much-needed defensive backing could take some time.
The Bills came up painfully short in their quest for a Super Bowl, and coach Sean McDermott got fired. They’re regarded as contenders largely because Josh Allen is always darting in and out of phone booths. But it’s well documented that he can’t do it alone. The Bills could experience some growing pains as Joe Brady attempts to make the big jump from offensive coordinator to head coach, and new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard tries to install a brand-new defense.
Ben Johnson ignited the Bears in his first season at the helm, and he helped Caleb Williams tap into some of the potential the franchise saw in the quarterback when selecting him No. 1 in 2024. Chicago’s defense led the NFL with 33 takeaways, and the Bears leapfrogged the Minnesota Vikings, Green Bay Packers and Detroit Lions in the division and reached the divisional round of the playoffs.
Expectations have skyrocketed, but taking that next step represents a great challenge. Williams delivered late-game heroics, but he and his team can’t count on a repeat of that trend. He’ll have to improve his consistency by a significant margin, and Chicago’s defense can’t get away with such a low pressure rate and such struggles against the run. The Bears feel primed for a step backward rather than forward.
The Eagles have ranked among the elite teams of the NFC for the last 10 years, making the playoffs nine times and winning the Super Bowl twice. Even with last season’s regression, they won the NFC East for the third time in four seasons.
But now they’re trying to re-tool on the fly, subtracting the disgruntled A.J. Brown and drafting Makai Lemon, rolling with their fourth offensive coordinator in as many years (rookie play caller Sean Mannion), and adding veterans Jonathan Greenard and Riq Woolen on defense while losing standouts Nakobe Dean and Reed Blankenship. The health of the offensive line is a concern, as is a tough late-season stretch . Although viewed as a bar-setter, the Eagles could hit a few snags this season.
The Patriots certainly exceeded expectations in 2025, overtaking Buffalo for the division and reaching the Super Bowl, where they lost to the Seattle Seahawks. Mike Vrabel and his players badly want to resolve unfinished business in 2026, but doing so could prove challenging.
New England will not have the luxury of sneaking up on teams this season. The Patriots also have a grueling start , with three road games in their first four weeks and two back-to-back road trips in their first 10 weeks. The Patriots landed A.J. Brown in hopes that he can help elevate Drake Maye, but chemistry could take some time. New England also still seems to lack a game-changing pass rush, which needs to change for their defense to take another step forward.

full_text:
John Harbaugh opens his first Giants training camp next week. Caleb Bowlin / Getty Images
Ingrid Harbaugh, self-proclaimed bird nerd, was in her suburban Baltimore yard when her Merlin app identified the first-time visitor flying alone as a common raven.
A few days later, right before her husband’s football team played the Pittsburgh Steelers for the AFC North title, Ingrid was stopped at a traffic light when she saw the very same bird.
“It was huge, and when it was swooping down, I thought it was going to hit the windshield,” she recalled in February. “It swooped over the car, and I looked in the rearview mirror and saw it sitting behind me in the street. I drove off with the bird sitting there before it flew off above the traffic.
“I said to John, ‘I wonder if that means the Ravens are in the rearview mirror, already behind us.’”
John Harbaugh wondered whether he had his own sign that the end of an 18-year run was near. He was reading the Book of Acts a couple of days before that win-or-else game in Pittsburgh when this New Testament line struck him: “His office let another take.”
Baltimore Ravens owner Steve Bisciotti took Harbaugh’s office after that 26-24 loss to the Steelers, and Harbaugh immediately turned his attention to the New York Giants. Even before he was fired, Harbaugh had ranked the Giants as his top choice among the teams expected to pursue him if he left Baltimore.
Harbaugh was aware the Giants had held internal discussions about his possible candidacy before their seasons had ended. He wanted them, and they wanted him.
Brian Daboll’s Giants were 13-38 over the last three years, and Harbaugh’s Ravens were 33-18. The Giants were 60 games under .500 over the last nine years, and Harbaugh was 41 games over .500 with Baltimore. The Giants have won only one playoff game over the last 14 years; Harbaugh had claimed eight of his 13 postseason victories, including a Super Bowl, in that time.
It seemed the perfect union of a coach who adored NFL history and a flagship franchise that had completely forgotten how to win. The Giants had past champs like Tom Coughlin, Eli Manning and Michael Strahan to sell Harbaugh on the glories of winning it all in New York. They had longtime senior executive Chris Mara to hold two private in-person meetings with Harbaugh and to persuade his brother, John, to give the coach the direct report to ownership he needed to take the job.
“We are going to compete for the playoffs and for championships,” John Harbaugh told The Athletic a half-hour after accepting. “I expect and want to make the playoffs next year.”
Harbaugh already knew it would be a monumental challenge to restore the Giants’ credibility before he endured an offseason that would surely remind him of just how far they have to go.
With the start of training camp a week away, Cam Skattebo’s viral backflip and tumble onto his rump at Fanatics Fest — after suffering a gruesome season-ending leg injury last fall — was a fitting punctuation mark on the six-month Harbaugh honeymoon, as it were.
When the coach saw the clip on his phone, he told Bob Papa and Carl Banks of the “Bleav in Giants” podcast that his reaction was: “Dude, at least stick it. You know what I mean? Land the thing if you’re going to do it.”
The Giants have missed a few landings since hiring Harbaugh, who has had his hands full while assembling a bigger, more physical team that he hopes will deliver the franchise’s first season of double-digit victories in a decade. The coach has answered questions about football and non-football concerns that he wished were never in play.
Football: The Giants’ best player, Dexter Lawrence, forced his way out of town. Three players suffered Achilles tendon tears in the spring. Malik Nabers criticized Harbaugh’s NFL Draft picks while his return from a serious knee injury remained a mystery.
Non-football: Co-owner Steve Tisch’s disclosed ties to Jeffrey Epstein blitzed Harbaugh before he’d even settled into the job. Jaxson Dart’s decision to introduce President Donald Trump at a Rockland County, N.Y., rally (without properly informing his employer of his role) compelled teammate Abdul Carter to criticize his quarterback on social media and moved Harbaugh to extinguish a spreading fire.
The good news is that Harbaugh, 63, has been coaching NFL or Division I college ball since 1984. He faced his share of on- and off-field crises in Baltimore, where, as a former Philadelphia Eagles assistant, he took over a divided team and a defense that wanted coordinator Rex Ryan to get the job.
Harbaugh had tense standoffs with legacy defenders Ed Reed, Ray Lewis and Terrell Suggs and, during the 2012 season, held a sitdown with his players to address their vicious and personal attacks on his approach. “The meeting we just had,” Harbaugh told them, “would happen in no other meeting room in the National Football League. There’s no other coach who would tolerate what was said in here.”
Those Ravens players went out and won the Super Bowl.
Harbaugh has seen the good, the bad and the ugly in the NFL, and he knows what buttons to push to inspire athletes to come together and achieve things they weren’t sure they could.
The bad news? The Giants’ young, talented players have become high-profile figures without winning games. Rookies Dart, Skattebo and Carter, who didn’t exactly produce a clean sheet as the No. 3 pick in the 2025 draft, all contributed to a 4-13 record a year after Nabers, the No. 6 pick in 2024, was a big part of a 3-14 team.
Did they happen to notice that Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns did their pro-wrestling thing after the Knicks’ drought-busting championship?
By the definition of his position, Dart is the Giants’ first-rounder who needs to be held to the highest standard. The franchise’s OG of Super Bowl coaches, Bill Parcells, used to tell Phil Simms: “I don’t need any celebrity quarterback. I need a battlefield commander.”
Dart is a modern-day Broadway Joe. He has every right to enjoy the spoils of New York in the social media age as long as he understands that every decision he makes — as a potential franchise quarterback — will impact the locker room, the coaching staff, the front office and the fan base.
Dart is a primary reason Harbaugh accepted the Giants’ $100 million offer. At Fanatics Fest, Dart said his new coach has had a profound impact on the team’s culture. “Like how Harbs establishes the camaraderie between the team, the coaching staff, the standard,” the quarterback said. “It’s a different feeling. It’s a refreshing feeling.”
But it’s a daunting feeling, too, for anyone who has watched Giants football for most of the last 15 years. Months before Mike Brown led the Knicks on their magical run, Coughlin told Harbaugh a ticker-tape parade in the big city “is the most incredible thing ever.”
Harbaugh had a vision of what that would look like. “I want to be in that parade,” he said in the winter. “But with that being said, what I’m thinking about is what the team looks like that earns the right to be in that parade someday. What do we have to build to get there? That’s what I’m really consumed with.”
After 18 years as a head coach in Baltimore and another 10 as an assistant in Philadelphia, the new guy believes he’s ready for this ultimate challenge. When practice starts next Wednesday at the Greenbrier Resort in West Virginia, millions of fans in the New York area will be wishing Harbaugh the best of luck.

full_text:
Braelon Allen (left) and Isaiah Davis will compete for carries behind Breece Hall. Vincent Carchietta / Imagn Images
The New York Jets might be coming off a three-win season, but there aren’t a lot of starting jobs up for grabs.
The best way to explain it: Many of the veterans the Jets signed in free agency are locked into starting jobs. The Jets also used three first-round picks on players who will contribute immediately, return four starting offensive linemen and brought back running back Breece Hall.
By my count, there are zero starting jobs available on offense, two on defense (three if you count nickel corner) and two on special teams.
The Jets also have some questions further down the depth chart where top backups will be decided, most notably at quarterback. Let’s start there as we dive into the roster battles to watch when training camp begins:
Contenders: Bailey Zappe, Cade Klubnik, Brady Cook
This spot, more than any other, feels like the one general manager Darren Mougey is most likely to add to. Maybe it will come during training camp, maybe after roster cuts, but at a minimum, it would surprise me if the Jets didn’t add someone.
It might not even be a player who would get fans excited, but one of these three quarterbacks needs to show a lot more in the early stretch of camp to have a legitimate shot to be Geno Smith’s top backup.
Zappe is the most experienced of the group with nine career starts. He got the bulk of the No. 2 reps during organized team activities.
Klubnik was just drafted in the fourth round and showed some intriguing flashes early in OTAs, but that was a low-pressure setting. He missed the latter part of OTAs and all of minicamp with a back injury. The best-case scenario for the Jets would be Klubnik having a good camp and preseason and outright winning the job.
Cook is a smart player and is respected by coaches and teammates, but he doesn’t appear to have the juice to be an NFL quarterback. He does have experience (153 pass attempts in five games last season), which Klubnik does not.
By the law of the New York Jets: If you are a quarterback on their roster or practice squad, you will probably play at some point.
Contenders: Braelon Allen, Isaiah Davis
This isn’t so much a “competition” like the others on this list since both backs will get opportunities to play.
However, I will be interested to see who falls second in the pecking order behind Hall once the season starts.
Allen was a summer star in each of his first two NFL seasons, though that hasn’t translated to the regular season. He looked like he was starting to build some momentum last season before suffering a season-ending injury in Week 4, but he’s completely healthy now and (according to him) stronger and faster than ever.
Davis isn’t a flashy player, and he’s not as big or strong as Allen, so their skill sets will be applied differently. However, Davis seems to get the job done when given the opportunity. He’s averaged 5.6 yards on 73 career carries and caught 30 of 40 passes thrown his way.
Contenders: Kiko Mauigoa, Marcelino McCrary-Ball, Mykal Walker
This is another position group that could use some reinforcements behind the starters. As it stands, in what should be predominantly a 3-4 defense, the thought of losing Jamien Sherwood or Demario Davis to injury is scary.
Mauigoa had some moments as a rookie, but it was a bumpy road, as he was forced to play before he was ready. McCrary-Ball and Walker are better suited as special-teams players than full-time contributors on defense.
Some notable free agents still available at linebacker include Bobby Okereke, Matt Milano, Kenneth Murray, Germaine Pratt and Elandon Roberts. Former Jets star Jamal Adams, most recently a linebacker for the Las Vegas Raiders, has also expressed interest in rejoining the team that drafted him.
Contenders: Nahshon Wright, Azareye’h Thomas, D’Angelo Ponds
This could be one of the most interesting competitions.
With Wright, the Jets have a veteran coming off a career season (five interceptions) with unique size (6 foot 4) and a playmaking skill set they were lacking. He also only signed for one year and $3.5 million, an indication there wasn’t a lot of interest in free agency.
However, the Jets have Thomas, a young, second-year cornerback they were high enough on a year ago to draft in the third round. His first start came when Sauce Gardner was injured. Thomas then stayed in the lineup for four more games after Gardner was traded before succumbing to a season-ending injury.
In those five games, he had five pass deflections and two tackles for loss but (like everyone else) no interceptions. He didn’t show enough to say he should be handed anything, but there is talent there.
Ponds got reps at both outside corner and nickel in the spring, so it’s always possible he impresses enough to get a shot to push Wright and Thomas, but he’s more likely to be in play at the nickel.
Contenders: Jarvis Brownlee, D’Angelo Ponds
This is an important job, but it won’t be as high-usage as you’d think for a nickel corner. The reason: Safety Minkah Fitzpatrick will get heavy usage in the nickel.
Still, the Jets would be smart to do what they can to get Ponds on the field. He already looked ready to make an impact in the spring even as a corner lacking in size, and his playmaking ability is something that should get him on the field quickly.
Brownlee came via an in-season trade with the Tennessee Titans in September and promptly forced the Jets’ first turnover of the season, but he succumbed to the same issues he had in Tennessee: penalties.
Contenders: Andre Cisco, Dane Belton, Malachi Moore
It was a surprise that the Jets brought back Cisco, but head coach Aaron Glenn still believes in him.
Cisco only played in eight games due to injuries and only mustered one fumble recovery, one pass deflection and one tackle for loss in those games. He signed for $2.23 million, not much more than the minimum.
I’d expect both Belton and Moore to give him a push for playing time. A year ago, Glenn was raving about how excited he was about Moore’s potential, and I don’t think his opinion of Moore has changed. Belton brings two things the Jets lacked on defense last season: a history of playmaking and sure-tackling.
Maybe Cisco will be the initial starter, but I’d bet on Belton and/or Moore eventually supplanting him.
Contenders: Jason Sanders, Cade York
Ah yes, the annual Jets kicking competition. Last year, the contenders (Harrison Mevis and Caden Davis) were bad enough that both were eventually cut.
Mougey signed Nick Folk during training camp, and Folk went on to be arguably the Jets’ best player. However, the Jets let Folk walk and got right back on the kicker carousel.
If Sanders is completely healed from a back injury that cost him the 2025 season, he should be an easy winner, having converted 37 of 41 field goals two years ago. York has only converted 73.3 percent in his career. If neither is up to the task, Mougey will go back to the drawing board again.
Contenders: Thomas Hennessy, Garrison Grimes
This is the first competition Hennessy has faced for the job in a long time. He currently holds the title of the longest-tenured Jets player, surviving coaching changes from Todd Bowles to Adam Gase to Robert Saleh to (on an interim basis) Jeff Ulbrich to Aaron Glenn.
The Jets signed Grimes as an undrafted rookie and have kept him on the roster, which means Glenn and special teams coordinator Chris Banjo are letting Grimes push Hennessy for the job.

full_text:
Vinod Khosla and Neeru Khosla, shown in 2017, are in line to become the Seattle Seahawks' next principal owners. Jesse Grant / Getty Images
The NFL keeps getting richer.
Earlier this month, the Paul Allen Estate agreed to sell the Seattle Seahawks to a group led by billionaire tech investor Vinod Khosla and his wife, Neeru Khosla, for $9.612 billion, a massive sum that exceeds the NFL’s previous record for a team sale by nearly 60 percent. As part of the agreement, which is subject to the approval of club owners at their Aug. 26 meeting in Atlanta, Neeru will serve as controlling owner and their son, Neal Khosla, will have “a significant leadership role,” according to an NFL memo sent to team executives and obtained by The Athletic .
The price tag alone says plenty about the NFL’s seemingly unbounded growth; it was only three years ago that the Washington Commanders sold for a then-record $6.05 billion. But the significance of the Seahawks deal extends beyond the financials. The Khoslas are entering a new chapter for the franchise after nearly three decades under the Allen family — bringing a similar tech and business legacy, but a very different personal history.
Vinod and Neeru Khosla were born in India and immigrated to the U.S. to continue their studies and launch careers as entrepreneurs. Vinod is now widely regarded as one of the most influential innovators and investors in Silicon Valley. In the NFL, the Khoslas will join the Vikings’ Zygi Wilf (Germany) and the Jaguars’ Shahid Khan (Pakistan) as the only other principal owners born outside the U.S.
Vinod, 71, received his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Technology in New Delhi, then earned his master’s in biomedical engineering from Carnegie Mellon University and in business administration from Stanford. Two years after getting his MBA, he co-founded Sun Microsystems, the pioneering computer company that reached a peak market capitalization of about $200 billion at the turn of the century.
Vinod, however, turned to investing in 1986 and is now widely regarded as one of the world’s leading technology venture capitalists, with an estimated net worth of $13.2 billion, according to Forbes’ latest billionaire rankings . He spent 18 years at Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers before launching his own firm in 2004. Khosla Ventures, a heavy backer of artificial intelligence along with climate and healthcare start-ups, was the first venture capital firm to invest in OpenAI. Now, seven years later, the company is valued around $852 billion .
“I would say the one piece that works really well in all business is go for high risk, higher consequences,” he told David Rubenstein in a 2022 interview for Bloomberg. “… I don’t mind a 90 percent probability of failure if there’s a 10 percent chance of changing the world.”
Vinod Khosla has built a career on taking risks and has repeatedly spoken about his own business failures, citing them as necessary tools for his successes. He’s also claimed that he’s a poor advisor on investing because “we’re really in this other business of company building” at Khosla Ventures.
But the NFL has proven to be one of the safest investments for the ultra-wealthy, and Khosla is on the verge of buying one of its most successful clubs.
“NFL valuations are going to keep going up, not because it’s about status but because the numbers justify it — the cash flows, the multiples of revenue,” said Marc Ganis, the founder of Sportscorp Ltd. and a consultant to multiple leagues and teams. “The NFL is arguably the best-run sports league in the world, and sports is playing a greater and greater role in global society and with technology.”
Neeru Khosla, once an aspiring doctor, grew up in India and England before joining Vinod in the U.S. She started in molecular biology, earning her master’s from San Jose State and working in gene expression research at a Stanford lab. But she stopped due to concern about being around radioactivity while pregnant with her first child (the Khoslas have four children). Her interest in education was born during her time as a volunteer at her children’s school. Neeru decided to go back to school at age 50 and earned another master’s degree, from Stanford Graduate School of Education, before launching CK-12 Foundation, a non-profit that provides free and customizable digital textbooks for children.
“As I went through that process with my four kids, I said, ‘Why didn’t I have education like this?’ That’s where the larger questions started coming up,” Neeru said in a 2013 interview with the Bridgespan Group. “Why is it that we cannot provide this kind of education for every kid? What stops us?”
Neeru adds to Seattle’s core of women sports owners, following Jody Allen, who has led the Seahawks since 2018, after the passing of her brother, Paul Allen. Samantha Holloway owns the Seattle Kraken and One Roof Sports and Entertainment, and is pushing to land an NBA expansion team in the city. Melinda French Gates recently became a minority investor in the Kraken and One Roof.
Neal Khosla, the only son of Vinod and Neeru, co-founded Curai Health, an AI-powered virtual care company. While studying mathematics and computer science at Stanford, he interned with the San Francisco 49ers’ football operations for two months, with a focus on the team’s draft process. He co-authored a research paper published by the Journal of Sports Management in 2014 that examined the determinants of live-game RSN ratings for the NBA, NHL and MLB.
Neal received his master’s in computer science from Stanford in 2016, and less than a year later launched Curai.
His “significant” involvement in the Seahawks, as the NFL memo described it, indicates he could be viewed as the future principal owner for the family. The NFL requires every club to file a succession plan and update it annually to try to ensure seamless transitions of power within families.
But in order to lead the Seahawks, the Khoslas will have to divest their 3.1 percent share in the 49ers, which they purchased last year. The NFL prohibits owners from holding interest in multiple franchises.
“My father and I have been season ticket holders for 30 years, going to games at the Stick starting when I was a child through the last 11 years at Levi’s Stadium,” Neal Khosla said in 2025. “For us, becoming members of the 49ers family is a dream come true and we’re honored to be a part of the team’s future success and continued impact on the Bay Area community.”
The Khoslas, who said in a statement attributed to Vinod earlier this month that they are “honored to be entrusted as the next stewards of the Seattle Seahawks,” declined to comment further for this story.
The NFL has tweaked its ownership policies over the years to make it easier for families to pass down franchises through generations and to make the purchase of teams slightly more attainable for new owners. In 2024, the league raised the debt limit to purchase a team to $1.4 billion and began to allow select private equity firms to invest up to 10 percent (non-control) in a team.
But the NFL, unlike the other American pro leagues, still requires an individual, not a group or institution, to be principal owner. That person must own at least 30 percent. (For teams owned by the same group for at least 10 years, the threshold for control is only 1 percent, provided the family collectively owns 30 percent.) The NFL also caps the number of limited partners for each team at 24 people.
The league’s restrictive policies have often raised the question of whether it will need to loosen them further to attract a broader pool of candidates who can afford its now-multibillion-dollar teams. Ganis believes NFL team values could reach $20 billion in the next seven years, requiring a principal owner to put down at least $6 billion to have control.
If the Seahawks deal proved anything, however, it’s that the league has so far not run into a shortage of billionaires…

title: Cardinals Starter Facing Multiple Charges After Guns And Gangs Investigation
full_text:
ARIZONA — A day before the Arizona Cardinals report for training camp, one of their returning starters finds himself in trouble.
According to TSN's Dave Naylor, Cardinals right guard Isaiah Adams has been charged with four different crimes related to a gun and gangs investigation.
"Arizona Cardinals OL Isaiah Adams listed among four people recently charged by Durham Regional Police following a guns and gangs investigation. Isaiah Derrick ADAMS, age 25 from Pickering is charged with: Possess Firearm Obtained by Crime, Possess Restricted/Prohibited Firearm – No Licence, and Possess Loaded Firearm, Possess Prohibited Device."
. @AZCardinals OL Isaiah Adams listed among four people recently  charged by Durham Regional Police following a guns and gangs investigation. Isaiah Derrick ADAMS, age 25 from Pickering is charged with: Possess Firearm Obtained by Crime, Possess Restricted/Prohibited Firearm –…
Adams started 11 games for the Cardinals last season and was a third-round pick in the 2024 NFL Draft.
In a statement acquired by Arizona Sports' Tyler Drake, the Cardinals said:
“We are aware of the situation involving Isaiah Adams. Out of respect for the process, we will refrain from commenting further at this time.”
More on the investigation from the Durham Regional Police:
"On Friday, July 17, 2026, investigators with the DRPS Guns and Gangs Unit concluded an investigation into a male believed to be in possession of a firearm and involved in drug trafficking.

Adams was set to enter a crucial third season in the NFL.

title: The Number That Could Finally End Cardinals, Jacoby Brissett Contract Battle
full_text:
ARIZONA — We're nearing the final hours before the Arizona Cardinals report to training camp on Wednesday, July 22 — and Jacoby Brissett's contract situation still isn't resolved.
It's been a storyline that's hung over the organization since the early beginnings of the offseason. After parting with Kyler Murray and whiffing on Malik Willis, the Cardinals deemed Brissett their starter for 2026.
Brissett, on the final year of his deal, wants more than the $1.5 million guaranteed on his contract. The Cardinals reportedly have been in agreement that a raise is due, though the two sides were far apart on what that number consists of.
"A day before the Cardinals report, and there is not yet a resolution to Jacoby Brissett’s contract situation," Ian Rapoport posted on X. "AZ and Brissett (who is his own agent) have been actively negotiating for the last several months and agree he’s due a raise. No consensus yet on the number."
Cardinals teammates have been vocal in their support of Brissett, the most recent coming from longtime team captain Budda Baker on social media:
Just want bro to get his shit done… he is not asking for what you think. Bro is asking for below the bare minimum. Let’s just get it done!!!
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur has backed Brissett at every opportunity when asked about the veteran quarterback, who hasn't participated in any OTA or minicamp practice but was spotted getting off-field work in recently with offensive stars in Trey McBride and Marvin Harrison Jr.
Arizona likely doesn't want to roll out rookie Carson Beck immediately while Gardner Minshew isn't exactly a top option, either. Brissett has an established rapport with the offense thanks to his 12 starts last season, a year where he went 1-11 as the team's starter despite putting up career-bests in passing yards and touchdowns.
The hang-up here is guaranteed money. Brissett doesn't want to be dubbed a starting quarterback and not be adequately paid like one, especially on the back half of a two-year deal that was essentially just supposed to be a backup quarterback contract.
In terms of total cash, Minshew is set to make just over $300,000 more than Brissett in 2026 (via Spotrac) . Minshew is set to have a guaranteed total of $5.14 million, far above Brissett's $1.5 million figure that does not include bonuses.
It does not seem as if Brissett wants more years added on to a deal: He wants more upfront dough guaranteed in the event that something happens. He's 33 and this could be his last opportunity to be a starting quarterback at the NFL level.
When looking at average quarterback guaranteed money per year entering the 2026 season, roughly $13 million is the estimate with names such as Baker Mayfield, Patrick Mahomes and Sam Darnold hovering around that line (per OverTheCap ).
Brissett's unique predicament makes this a tough projection. He's not close to any of the three quarterbacks in terms of talent nor is he on a multi-year deal or part of a franchise's future plans.
Brissett very likely is eying at least $10 million in guarantees, which would tie him for the lowest non-rookie amount alongside Kirk Cousins (h/t Josh Weinfuss, ESPN ).
That appears to be the golden number. Arizona, who likely will turn to another quarterback at some point in the 2026 season, probably isn't keen to make that happen.
And alas, the ongoing game of chicken continues to the final moments before the Cardinals report at State Farm Stadium.
Will Brissett settle for anything less than $10 million guaranteed? That's the new question, one that could be resolved in a matter of either hours or weeks.

title: Cardinals Roster Tiers, Part 6: The Difference-Makers
full_text:
Welcome to the second tier of our Arizona Cardinals roster rankings ahead of training camp. If you've missed any of the previous tiers, you can click on them below:
We've reached the second-to-last tier of the pyramid. It's been a fun ride, though only a total of seven players exist in the top two groups. Today we'll evaluate Arizona's trio of veteran difference-makers.
Three staples. Three defensive players. Three leaders in terms of their position group and overall level of play.
As a reminder, the players are not ranked within the tier itself.
Players in this tier : Budda Baker, Josh Sweat, Mack Wilson Sr.
Baker has been the engine of Arizona's defense for years now, making the Pro Bowl in all but one of his nine years in the NFL. He doesn't post flashy interception numbers but is a productive tackler and has free rein within Nick Rallis' defense to attack when/wherever — which is a privilege afforded to few.
That helps keep opposing offensive coordinators guessing, and Baker's role as a leader through another coaching staff change can't be overstated. He's still viewed as one of the top safeties in the league and will be the heart and soul of the Cardinals until he decides otherwise.
Sweat's sack production (12.5) in his first season with Arizona was second to none and probably deserved Pro Bowl recognition. Sweat is far and away the top (and only) pass rush threat in Arizona's outside linebacker room, and the Cardinals' willingness to leave his room untouched only heightens Sweat's importance to the team.
Without Jonathan Gannon in the desert, it will be interesting to see how Sweat builds on one of his best years in the league. However, no defense can thrive without a pass rush, and Sweat's the undisputed top person to reach the quarterback in Arizona.
Wilson isn't quite on the same star-name level as Baker or Sweat, though if you ever needed to evaluate his importance to Arizona's defense — you can take a look at last season. The Cardinals were night and day different after Wilson went down with a season-ending rib injury. The front seven looked like a shell of itself.
Wilson's a versatile athlete at inside linebacker that handles captain and green dot duties for the Cardinals. He's effective against the run, rushing the passer and dropping into coverage, too. There's not much Wilson can't do, and while he's not a Pro Bowl player (yet), he sure plays like it.
Wilson wears many hats for the Cardinals in terms of responsibility, and when healthy, he's a glue guy for Arizona's defense.
